title: Build a divider bias bench
concept: An operating point solves the steady voltages and currents of the fixture. Put the resistor divider in its own cell and apply 1 V from the parent fixture.
question: With equal resistors and no additional output load, where does a 1 V input put the divider output?
explanation: The two equal resistors split the applied voltage equally.
work: Select XDUT and choose Schematic → Enter schematic. Select R2 and change Value to 1k in its properties so it matches R1. Choose Schematic → Return to parent and trace VIN, out and return net 0.
reflection: Explain where you set the 1 V input, where you set R2, and where you told the solver to check the output.

title: Sweep the divider input
concept: A DC sweep solves a series of operating points. Each point reuses the same fixture with a different value on the selected independent source.
question: What slope does the ideal equal-resistor divider have when you plot output voltage against input voltage?
explanation: The output stays at half the input throughout the sweep.
work: Open the DC fixture. Identify VIN as the swept voltage source and confirm it drives the same XDUT divider you repaired in the previous lesson.
reflection: Use two points from the sweep to explain the slope. What physical input quantity does the horizontal axis represent?

title: Measure a loaded divider step
concept: A capacitor on the output makes the response time-dependent. The capacitor sees the two 1 kΩ resistors in parallel, so its 2 nF load gives a time constant of 1 µs.
question: What does adding the output capacitor change for this ideal step?
options: The time needed to reach the final voltage
explanation: The capacitor draws charging current during the transition and no current after the DC output settles.
work: Open the step fixture. Locate CLOAD on out and inspect VIN’s 0–1 V pulse. Its leading edge starts at 2 µs.
reflection: Compare your 3 µs reading with the final voltage. Explain why replacing CLOAD would change one of those readings more than the other.

title: Set the TIA bias and photocurrent
concept: The feedback resistor converts current into voltage. With the input held near a 0.9 V reference, 1 µA through 100 kΩ moves the output down by about 0.1 V for this current direction.
question: Increasing the photocurrent in the supplied fixture moves the output in which direction?
explanation: The output moves down to conduct the injected current through the feedback resistor.
work: Trace IPHOTO through VSENSE to the summing node, then trace RF back from out. Select IPHOTO and set its DC value to 1u in its properties. Keep RF at 100k.
reflection: Explain the sign of the output change and calculate the ideal voltage shift from the photocurrent and feedback resistance.

title: Measure TIA transimpedance
concept: An AC analysis linearizes around the bias point. For a 1 µA AC input, an output magnitude of 0.1 V corresponds to 100 kΩ of transimpedance.
question: Which unit describes the ratio of TIA output voltage to input current?
explanation: Voltage divided by current has units of ohms.
work: Select RF and set Value to 100k. Select IPHOTO and confirm its AC amplitude is 1u. Keep CPD between sense and ground and CF between out and sense.
reflection: Convert your 100 Hz voltage to ohms using the AC current. Explain what the high-frequency rolloff would imply for a fast optical signal.

title: Test a photodiode current step
concept: The pulse fixture models a change in light as a current step. Observing both the settling waveform and the final output checks the feedback network under a time-domain stimulus.
question: Which result shows whether the TIA rings immediately after a current step?
options: The DC sweep at its last point
explanation: The transient waveform preserves the time history around the edge.
work: Open the pulse fixture. Confirm RF is 100k and IPHOTO rises from 0 to 1 µA at 10 µs. Identify the output node and both feedback components.
reflection: Compare the output before and after the current edge. What does the transition tell you that the final 30 µs reading alone cannot show?

title: Bias a two-stage amplifier as a follower
concept: A practical amplifier bench supplies power, common-mode input, a bias current and a load. Unity feedback gives a useful operating-point check before more involved tests.
question: Where do you connect the inverting input to make a unity-gain follower?
explanation: Connecting the output to the inverting input closes the negative-feedback loop.
work: Open the follower fixture. Confirm XDUT’s INN and OUT share out. Verify VIN is 0.9 V, VDD is 1.8 V and IREF supplies 5 µA.
reflection: Describe why the output sits near the input when the loop is closed. Record the input, supply and bias-current settings.

title: Build the amplifier AC loop bench
concept: The large inductor keeps the feedback path closed at DC. The capacitor holds the feedback node near AC ground, letting the 1 V small-signal stimulus expose the amplifier’s gain.
question: Why keep a path for DC feedback in the AC loop fixture?
options: To preserve the intended operating point
To make the supply part of the input signal
explanation: AC analysis uses the circuit’s DC bias point before it evaluates the small-signal response.
work: Select CL and change Value to 1p. Trace LDC from out to feedback and CAC from feedback to ground. Select VIN and verify its AC amplitude is 1.
reflection: Use the output magnitude and AC input to report low-frequency gain. Explain why the AC plot can show more than 1.8 V of magnitude while the circuit still operates from a 1.8 V supply.

title: Check follower step response under load
concept: The unity-gain step fixture checks whether the feedback loop can move the output with its load connected. A late output sample is a check on the final level, alongside the full waveform.
question: Why inspect the waveform as well as measuring the final level?
options: The waveform shows overshoot and ringing
The final voltage sets the process corner
The waveform changes the load capacitor
explanation: Different transient responses can have the same settled output.
work: Open the follower step fixture. Check that VIN rises from 0.85 to 0.95 V at 5 µs and that CL is 1p. Verify that INN remains tied to out.
reflection: Describe the shape of the step and compare the before and after voltage. If you saw overshoot, explain how the settled sample could still pass.

title: Build a balanced differential stimulus
concept: Use two complementary sources so the differential voltage changes sign at a fixed common mode.
question: How do you make a 0.10 V differential signal about 0.90 V common mode?
options: Drive one input to 0.95 V and the other to 0.85 V
Drive one input to 0.10 V and ground the other
explanation: The average of the two inputs is common mode; their difference is the differential voltage.
work: Edit VMINUS so its pulse goes from 0.95 V to 0.85 V at 4 µs. Keep VPLUS rising from 0.85 V to 0.95 V. Check both nets.
reflection: Record both input levels, their average and their difference before and after the transition. Explain why a single-ended reading is insufficient.
